concepts.title: A Just and Placid City, an Arch and a Falling Crown
concepts.definition: Vikram Seth narrates in mock-heroic verse the tale of a just and placid city where the king orders an arch built over the main thoroughfare. Riding under it, the king strikes his head -- the crown falls -- and he demands the culprit be hanged, launching an absurd chain of blame.
concepts.key_idea: One bump, one crown, one decree -- a satire of justice begins with a low arch.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp105.txt opening verses (just and placid city, arch over thoroughfare, king strikes head, crown falls, culprit to be hanged)
question_patterns: what happened when the king rode under the arch

why is the arch important in the poem

solution_steps.explain: A placid, just king builds a fine arch -- vanity and civic pride in one structure.
The arch stands too low; the king's crown is knocked off as he rides beneath.
Humiliated before his subjects, the king orders the guilty party hanged -- inviting an endless relay of blame.

concepts.title: The Culprit Hunt up to the King
concepts.definition: The workmen blame the masons, the masons blame the architect, and the architect blames the king -- who had altered the plans. The flustered king widens his decree to 'hang whoever fits the noose', and by the noose's own measurement the tallest man present, the king himself, is chosen.
concepts.key_idea: Blame climbs the ladder to the throne -- and the king's own widened decree pulls the noose to his neck.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp105.txt blame verses (workmen blame masons, architect blames the king, culprit catcher, decree widened, noose fits the king)
question_patterns: trace the chain of culprits from the workmen to the king
in class 11 the tale of melon city: how did the architect save himself

how does the poet use irony in the trial scene

solution_steps.explain: Workmen blame masons, masons blame the architect, and the architect reminds them the king amended the plans.
Unable to judge his own guilt, the king asks the crowd for guidance and widens the decree to whoever fits the noose.
The noose fits only one man -- the tall king -- and the just and placid monarch is hanged by his own command.

concepts.title: The Melon Crown: Satire on Passive Governance
concepts.definition: The ministers proceed to crown the next man who passes the city gate -- which the principles of the land require -- and the passer-by turns out to be a melon. The city accepts its melon king without complaint, calling it all right, and lives in peace: Seth's satire on people who ask nothing of a state and get exactly what they tolerate.
concepts.key_idea: A melon wears the crown because nobody minds -- the sharpest joke on subjects who never question.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp105.txt closing verses (melon crowned king, next man passing the gate, principles of the land, all right say the citizens, moral on just and placid people)

solution_steps.action: follow the law of the gate
solution_steps.explain: By the city's principles, whoever passes the gate next shall choose the king -- and that passer-by is a melon.
The melon is carried in state and crowned without protest; governance continues undisturbed.
Peace without justice, obedience without questions -- Seth mocks subjects placid enough to be ruled by fruit.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain how the king becomes the victim of his own decree in the trial scene.

solution_template.explain: His first order -- hang the culprit -- fails as blame keeps escaping upward.
To satisfy the crowd he generalises: hang whoever fits the noose, no questions asked.
Only his own tall frame fills the noose, so his arbitrary standard selects the lawgiver himself.

worked_examples.question_pattern: The citizens say of their melon king, 'it is all right'. What does this remark reveal about them and about the poem's message?

solution_template.explain: No one examines whether a melon can rule; contentment replaces judgment.
A placid people gets a placid state -- governance mirrors the governed.
Seth warns that citizens who never demand sense will be governed by nonsense -- peacefully, but absurdly.
